title: Literal Characters
lesson: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern used to find text. The simplest pattern is a literal match. The pattern ruby matches the letters 'r', 'u', 'b', 'y' in that exact sequence, and is case-sensitive.
task: Match the word ruby (lowercase) in the target string.
hint: Literal patterns match themselves. Type exactly 'ruby' to pass.

title: Wildcard Dot
lesson: The dot . is a wildcard character that matches any single character (letters, digits, symbols, spaces) except a newline. For example, d.g matches 'dog', 'dig', 'dug', or even 'd#g'.
task: Match cat, cot, and cut with a single pattern using the wildcard dot.
hint: Replace the middle vowel with a dot: c.t

title: Character Classes
lesson: Square brackets [...] define a character class. It matches any single character enclosed within the brackets. E.g., b[ae]t matches 'bat' and 'bet', but not 'bit'.
task: Match bat and bet, but do NOT match bit.
hint: Put the permitted vowels inside brackets: b[ae]t

title: Ranges in sets
lesson: Instead of listing every letter or number, you can specify ranges using a hyphen - inside square brackets. E.g., [a-z] matches any lowercase letter, and [0-9] matches any digit.
task: Match any single lowercase letter between 'p' and 's' (p, q, r, s).
hint: Write the character set range using a hyphen: [p-s]

title: Negated Sets
lesson: Adding a caret ^ as the first character inside square brackets negates the class. E.g., [^0-9] matches any single character that is NOT a digit.
task: Match any word ending in 'ot' EXCEPT the word not.
hint: Negate 'n' in the character set before 'ot': [^n]ot

title: Start Anchor
lesson: Outside square brackets, the caret ^ anchors the pattern to the beginning of a line or string. E.g., ^cat matches 'cat' only if it is the very first word.
task: Match Hello only when it starts the line.
hint: Put the caret at the start of your pattern: ^Hello

title: End Anchor
lesson: The dollar sign $ anchors the pattern to the end of a line or string. E.g., dog$ matches 'dog' only if it is the last word in the string.
task: Match Dojo only when it ends the line.
hint: Put the dollar sign at the end of your pattern: Dojo$

title: The Plus Quantifier
lesson: The plus + matches one or more repetitions of the preceding character or group. For example, go+al matches 'goal' and 'gooal', but not 'gal'.
task: Match hooray with any number of 'o's (must have at least one 'o').
hint: Use the plus quantifier on the 'o' character: ho+ray

title: The Star Quantifier
lesson: The asterisk * matches zero or more repetitions of the preceding character or group. E.g., ab*c matches 'ac', 'abc', and 'abbc'.
task: Match ac, abc, and abbc with a single pattern using the star quantifier.
hint: Place the asterisk after the optional repeating 'b': ab*c

title: Optional Question Mark
lesson: The question mark ? makes the preceding character or group optional (matches 0 or 1 time). E.g., colors? matches 'color' and 'colors'.
task: Match both American color and British colour spellings.

title: Range Quantifiers
lesson: Curly braces {n,m} match between n and m repetitions of the preceding item. {n} matches exactly n times. {n,} matches n or more times.
task: Match exactly 3 digits in a row.
hint: Use a digit set [0-9] and the quantifier {3}.

title: Digit Shortcuts
lesson: Regex provides shortcuts for common character sets. \d matches any single digit (equivalent to [0-9]). \w matches any word character (alphanumeric and underscore). \s matches whitespace.
task: Match a 3-digit number using the digit shortcut \d.
hint: Combine \d with a curly brace quantifier: \d{3}

title: Grouping and Alternation
lesson: Parentheses (...) group terms, and the pipe | acts as an 'OR' operator. For example, (red|blue) matches 'red' or 'blue'.
task: Match red, green, or blue using grouping and alternation.
hint: Put the colors inside parentheses separated by pipes: (red|green|blue)

title: Word Boundaries
lesson: The boundary anchor \b asserts a position where a word character is next to a non-word character (like spaces, punctuation, or start/end of string). E.g., \bcat\b matches 'cat' but not 'cats' or 'bobcat'.
task: Match the word cat exactly, preventing matches inside other words.
hint: Wrap the literal word 'cat' in word boundaries: \bcat\b

title: Lookahead Assertions
lesson: A positive lookahead (?=...) matches a position followed by a pattern, but does NOT include it in the match result. E.g., \d+(?=px) matches digits only if they are immediately followed by 'px'.
task: Match any numeric value only if followed immediately by the unit usd.
hint: Use digits quantifier \d+ followed by positive lookahead (?=usd)
